body.text: Ghulam Sofi’s forehead bears a dark mark right in the center; it is from years of offering namaz, he says. It is Friday and Sofi is getting ready for the prayers at his home in the Khanyar area of Indian-administered Kashmir’s Srinagar city.

As Sofi neatly adjusts his skullcap, without ruining the thin layer of grey hair under it, he says, “In Kashmir, Islam and politics have always remained inseparable. We can smell the link this time too.”
Sofi is referring to the recent order by Kashmir’s Waqf Board, a body overseeing Muslim shrines in the region.

On October 10, the Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board – headed by Dr. Syed Darakhshan Andrabi, a Kashmiri leader associated with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu supremacist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) – proposed developing common themes for Friday sermons across mosques and shrines in the conflicted region. Soon after the news of the homogenizing of sermons spread, it came under fire for political interference in religious affairs. Locals feel that the board’s plan to dictate Friday sermons is an assault on their faith, dressed up as “coordination.”
Policing the Pulpit
The order to homogenize sermon themes has been widely read alongside the backdrop of a broader political shift.

In 2019, when the Modi government revoked Kashmir’s special constitutional status and brought the region under direct central rule, institutions underwent sweeping legal and administrative changes, including the Waqf Board, which administers Muslim religious endowments and properties.

In 2022, a new board was constituted under India’s central Waqf framework, with BJP leader Andrabi appointed chairperson. The board directly administers fewer than 150 mosques and shrines in the region, out of the thousands that exist, but it set out an ambitious proposal for Friday sermons at all of Kashmir’s mosques.

“The Waqf Board’s move to prescribe uniform Friday sermons is deeply problematic because it amounts to interference in the religious affairs of the Muslim community,” Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, the region’s top Muslim religious leader, told The Diplomat. “The pulpit of a mosque is a sacred trust, and the responsibility of delivering religious guidance rests with the Islamic clerics and recognized religious institutions. Imposing sermons through a government-appointed body disregards this tradition and raises serious questions about religious autonomy.”

Farooq urged caution on the interference. “The pulpit is not an instrument of the state. Any attempt to control or dictate its message, directly or indirectly, is unacceptable. Our position is not against coordination or reform, but against the state assuming authority over matters that rightly belong to the religious community and its scholars,” he said.

Jammu and Kashmir’s Chief Minister Omar Abdullah criticized the idea and the agenda behind it. “This is an unacceptable attempt by the BJP to interfere in the religious affairs of Muslims and will not be accepted under any circumstances,” he said. “The BJP-appointed chairperson must immediately halt this misplaced attempt to please her masters.”

Heavy backlash from many corners – from politicians to pulpits of different Islamic sects in the region – forced Andrabi to backtrack. While Andrabi, whose X profile showcases a photo of her with Modi, defended the move, she said that it was only a proposal and there was no order in place.
But the potential syncing of sermons is not the only act that has attempted to intervene in the functioning of Islamic institutions in the valley.
After Revocation of Rights

After the abrogation of Jammu and Kashmir’s special status in 2019, the lieutenant governor (LG)’s administration took control over various spheres of society. In the beginning, the LG banned 215 community-run Islamic schools that had operated for more than five decades and serve largely low- and middle-income families.

The Indian state’s first acts after August 5, 2019, were not limited to detaining political leaders and imposing a communications blackout. They extended to policing Kashmir’s mosques and clerics to prevent opposition to the abrogation of Article 370. At the time, authorities also barred congregational Friday and Eid prayers at prominent shrines, deployed security forces outside mosques, detained clerics, and summoned them to army camps, where they were instructed to counsel people against protesting and warned them against discussing Article 370 in their sermons.

A police circular issued shortly before August 5 had also sought details of mosques and their management committees across Srinagar. This stirred an atmosphere of surveillance and revealed how deeply the Indian state associated the possibility of rebellion in Kashmir with Islamic institutions. Mosques were treated as potential centers of political mobilization.

In January 2026, police carried out surveillance operations in which they profiled all mosques and affiliated people. Mosque clerics in several neighborhoods across Kashmir, were asked to fill out forms listing names of attendees, phone numbers, and institutional details – a process that has left them unsure how Kashmir’s Islamic spaces are now being viewed by the Indian state.

While locals say that mosque profiling was not a new activity by the state, the extremely invasive nature of profiling this time caused alarm. The authorities sought information such as the physical structure of the mosque, cost of construction, source of funds, monthly expenditure, and income. It also sought shockingly detailed information about the people associated with the mosques, including their financial status, and bank, passport, ATM, and credit card details.
Muslims constitute more than 97 percent of the population in the Kashmir Valley and almost 68 percent in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir.

In September of this year, the Waqf Board restricted devotees from bringing and distributing food items and feeding birds inside the premises of Waqf-managed shrines. The move drew flak since both aspects are traditionally rooted in Kashmir’s shrine culture.

The board showcases its actions as efforts to protect religious properties, improve transparency, and preserve Kashmir’s Sufi heritage. However, these changes raise concerns about what happens when authority over Muslim religious institutions shifts from locally embedded custodians to the India-controlled bureaucracy, which even the United States has termed as dangerous for Muslims. The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) has repeatedly criticized India’s Waqf legislation, categorizing it as part of a broader pattern of state encroachment on the religious autonomy of Muslims.
Conversion, Conflict, and Chaos

In April 2024, Sandeep Kumar, a resident of northern India’s Haryana state, accepted Islam voluntarily in Kashmir’s Hazratbal shrine, in the presence of tens of thousands of people. Kumar, who converted from Hinduism to Islam, was administered the oath by Dr. Kamaluddin Farooqui, the head cleric at the shrine since 2018.

J&K police hurriedly lodged a complaint against Farooqui for presiding over the alleged “forced conversion.” Later, Farooqui was removed by the Waqf Board under Andrabi for presiding over a public conversion of a Hindu man to Islam, even though Kumar said he was acting voluntarily. Last month, Farooqui approached the court seeking reinstatement. His family had served as hereditary preachers at the shrine for generations.

Farooqui said that the issue involving himself should compel Kashmiris to examine a much larger question: who ultimately decides the future of Kashmir’s religious institutions. “Our faith is not a political project. Our mosques are not instruments of government and the right to ask questions must never be mistaken for disloyalty,” he told The Diplomat.

In September 2025, the installation of India’s national emblem at Hazratbal shrine triggered worshippers who attempted to destroy the newly installed plaque, saying it did not belong at the shrine. The crowd’s anger was rooted in the fact that the emblem features animals, which goes against Islamic teachings that ban idol worship. This too, exposed tensions over religious sanctity and state authority within sacred spaces.
Hazratbal shrine has long been a site where religious devotion, Kashmiri political identity, and resistance to Indian rule have intersected.

The shrine’s political significance predates the region’s armed insurgency of the late 1980s. In the decades that followed, Kashmiri leaders hosted large political congregations, while separatist leaders also called for demonstrations from Hazratbal. In October 1993, Indian security forces laid siege to the shrine after anti-India rebels took shelter inside, triggering a prolonged standoff and a 35-day shutdown called by the All Parties Hurriyat Conference in protest.

In July 2008, separatist leaders including Shabir Ahmad Shah and Mohammad Ashraf Sehrai addressed thousands at Hazratbal after a call issued by one of Kashmir’s most towering pro-freedom leaders, Syed Ali Shah Geelani.

In 2016, during the unrest that followed the killing of extremist group Hizbul Mujahideen’s commander Burhan Wani, the Joint Resistance Leadership – comprising Geelani, Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, and Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front Chairman Mohammad Yasin Malik – called for a march to Hazratbal to offer Friday prayers and held a public rally in memory of those killed in the protests.

In Kashmir, where religious identity is inseparable from a longer struggle over political autonomy and cultural belonging, pulpits have been points of political friction. But Farooqui said that one cannot ignore the concern that political influence may be reshaping the administration of Kashmir’s mosques and shrines.

“But one principle must remain non-negotiable: neither the BJP nor any other political party should be permitted to use administrative authority to dictate religious life in Kashmir,” he said. “Are our mosques being governed by the law and the will of the people, or by a political agenda? Kashmir’s faith cannot be held hostage to political power. The people deserve answers, not silence.”
